title: The First Morning
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 33 of 40
content:
The first morning I woke beside Severus Snape, he was already awake.

Of course he was.

He lay on his back staring at the ceiling with the expression of a man conducting a hostile review of existence.

I blinked at him.

“Good morning.”

His eyes moved toward me.

“Debatable.”

I smiled into the pillow.

We had spent the night at Spinner's End.

Not accidentally.

Not because a storm trapped us or the Floo failed or some emergency made privacy convenient.

We had chosen it.

That distinction had mattered enough that Snape asked twice before closing the bedroom door.

What followed belonged to us and not to an audience. There had been kissing, nervous laughter mostly mine, a surprising amount of negotiation, and eventually the kind of intimacy that made language unnecessary.

We had gone slowly.

We had stopped once.

We had started again because we both wanted to.

Now morning made everything ordinary in the most alarming way.

His hair was everywhere.

One side had flattened against the pillow. The other stood at an angle I had never seen in public.

I stared.

“No,” he said.

I laughed.

“You look—”

“Finish that sentence carefully.”

“Human.”

His eyes narrowed.

“Disappointing, I know.”

“Profoundly.”

I moved closer.

He went still for the smallest second before relaxing.

Morning touch, I realized, was new territory.

Last night every contact had been asked in explicit language.

Now I let my hand rest on the blanket between us.

“Can I?”

His gaze dropped to it.

“Yes.”

I touched his shoulder.

Then his chest.

Nothing sexual.

Just warm skin and the rhythm of his breathing beneath my palm.

His hand covered mine.

“This is strange,” he said.

“What is?”

“You being here.”

“Bad strange?”

He considered.

“No.”

“Good strange?”

“Do not make me use that phrase.”

“Neutral strange?”

“Unfamiliar.”

That was more honest.

I nodded.

“Me too.”

His eyebrows rose.

“What?”

“You appear comfortable.”

“I am performing competence.”

His mouth curved.

“Recognizable technique.”

We stayed in bed longer than either of us usually allowed ourselves.

Snape pretended this was because the room was cold.

I pretended to believe him.

Eventually the kettle downstairs whistled on a timing charm.

He closed his eyes.

“You enchanted the kettle?”

“Yes.”

“For what time?”

“Seven.”

I looked at the clock.

“It is seven.”

“I am aware.”

“You planned morning tea.”

“I plan most things.”

“Romantic.”

He pulled the blanket over his face.

I laughed so hard I had to sit up.

“This relationship is intolerable,” he said from beneath the blanket.

“You're hiding.”

“I am reconsidering.”

“Agreement two. No disappearing as strategy.”

The blanket lowered.

His eyes were amused.

“I hate that document.”

“You wrote half of it.”

“An error.”

We went downstairs.

The kitchen was cold, but sunlight reached the table. Snape brewed tea. I found bread and eggs. He objected to my method of cooking eggs.

“You are stirring too aggressively.”

“They are eggs.”

“Texture remains relevant.”

“You're not allowed to turn breakfast into Potions.”

“Everything involving heat, timing, and ingredients has standards.”

“Should I use a silver cauldron?”

“Do not be ridiculous. Copper would distribute heat better.”

I stared.

He stared back.

Then we both started laughing.

It was absurdly domestic.

That frightened me a little.

I realized it while buttering toast.

The feeling must have crossed my face because Snape stopped criticizing the eggs.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

His eyebrow rose.

I sighed.

“This is nice.”

His expression became wary.

“Yes.”

“And nice can become expected.”

He waited.

“And expected can become required.”

Understanding moved through his face.

“You are afraid of obligation.”

“Sometimes.”

“Of me?”

“Not exactly.”

He set down his cup.

“Explain exactly.”

I smiled faintly.

“You really hate ambiguity.”

“Yes.”

I leaned against the counter.

“I don't want waking up here to become something either of us has to do to prove we're serious.”

Snape considered.

“No.”

“No?”

“It will not.”

“That simple?”

“Yes.”

He picked up his cup.

I stared.

“You're good at this sometimes.”

“Do not spread the rumor.”

Warmth returned.

I put the eggs on plates.

Snape tasted them.

“Well?”

He chewed with maddening deliberation.

“Acceptable.”

I threw a napkin at him.

He caught it.

After breakfast, we dressed.

Snape's shirt collar caught against the scar on his throat. He hissed and pulled it away.

I watched his hand tremble.

“Help?” I asked.

A pause.

“Yes.”

I stepped close.

He stood still while I fastened the top buttons more loosely and folded the collar so it did not rub.

My fingers moved near the scar without touching it.

His breathing stayed even.

“Better?”

“Yes.”

I smoothed the fabric once over his shoulder.

He looked at me.

“You are staring.”

“I like you.”

“That is not a defense.”

“I love you.”

His face immediately betrayed him.

Color.

Softness.

Annoyance at both.

“That is even less relevant.”

“I disagree.”

He kissed my forehead.

Quickly, as if hoping to escape consequences.

I caught his coat before he could step away.

“Again.”

His eyebrow rose.

“Demanding.”

“Yes.”

He kissed me properly.

When we finally left the house, he locked the door and stood on the pavement beside me.

“Tonight?” he asked.

Not an expectation.

A question.

I thought about my own room at Hogwarts, my work, the pleasure of missing someone by choice rather than obligation.

“Tomorrow,” I said.

Snape nodded.

“Tomorrow.”

No hurt.

No punishment.

Just a plan.

The first morning did not turn us into one person.

It gave us breakfast, bad hair, careful questions, and a door we could leave separately.

For me, that was more romantic than destiny.
